title: Team Crisis Manager
theme: Stakeholder Alignment & Team Leadership Under Pressure
description: You are the project lead on a high-stakes product launch. Four AI teammates each represent a different priority — budget, timeline, quality, and team morale. Every decision you make satisfies some teammates and frustrates others. Can you align competing interests and lead your team to a successful launch without losing anyone's trust?
learning_objectives: Navigate competing stakeholder priorities without dismissing any one perspective
Understand that leadership means holding tension between contradictory needs
Practice empathy by seeing situations through each teammate's lens
Learn to communicate decisions transparently even when unpopular
Develop resilience when satisfying everyone is impossible

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are the project lead. Your 4 teammates each care deeply about one thing.
Alex cares about Budget. Sam cares about Timeline. Jordan cares about Quality. Morgan cares about Team Morale.
Each round presents a crisis. Your choice affects the team differently — someone always wins, someone always loses.
Watch your 4 team trust bars. If any drops to zero, the team fractures.
Complete all 8 rounds to deliver the project. Your final score is based on how balanced your team relationships are.
tips: You cannot satisfy everyone every round — that is the point
The best leaders rotate who they prioritize so no one is always last
Explain your reasoning — even bad news lands better with transparency
Morgan's morale affects everyone; ignoring it has compounding costs

psychological_framework.description: Team leadership requires holding multiple valid perspectives simultaneously — a core empathy and systems-thinking skill.

core_skills.name: Empathy
core_skills.description: Genuinely understanding what each person needs and why

core_skills.name: Adaptability
core_skills.description: Shifting approach based on who needs support most right now

core_skills.name: Strategic Thinking
core_skills.description: Seeing the bigger picture when immediate pressures feel urgent

core_skills.name: Resilience
core_skills.description: Staying composed when you cannot give everyone what they want

glossary_terms.definition: Anyone with a stake in the outcome of your work — often with different priorities.
glossary_terms.example: Your finance team and your engineering team both care about the product but for different reasons.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Stakeholder theory, developed by Edward Freeman, argues that sustainable organizations must balance the interests of all parties affected by their decisions — not just shareholders.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: When Satya Nadella took over Microsoft, he mapped out every stakeholder — employees, customers, developers, investors — and adjusted strategy to address each group's most critical concern.

glossary_terms.definition: The collective emotional state of a team — how energized, trusted, and motivated they feel.
glossary_terms.example: A team with high morale ships faster, makes fewer errors, and handles setbacks better.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Google's Project Aristotle (2015) found that psychological safety — knowing you won't be punished for speaking up — was the single most important factor in team performance.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Netflix famously gives employees unlimited vacation not as a perk, but because they found that autonomy and trust are the highest morale drivers for knowledge workers.

glossary_terms.definition: The cost of choosing one option is giving up another — there is no free lunch in decisions.
glossary_terms.example: Choosing speed (timeline) usually costs quality or team wellbeing.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: In decision theory, every choice has an opportunity cost — the value of the next-best alternative you gave up. Skilled leaders make trade-offs consciously rather than pretending they do not exist.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Apple historically chose quality over speed, often delaying products rather than shipping something imperfect — a conscious trade-off that built their brand reputation.

halftime_config.reflection_question: Which teammate have you been neglecting most? Why?
halftime_config.custom_message: Halfway through the project. Look at your team trust scores — is anyone close to breaking point?

rounds.title: The Scope Creep Problem
rounds.story: The product manager just added 12 new features to the launch scope — three days before the sprint ends. Alex says the budget cannot absorb the extra engineering hours. Sam says the timeline is already red. Jordan says cutting corners on testing will break the product. Morgan says the team is already exhausted and adding more work could cause burnout. The PM is waiting for your call.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle unexpected scope expansion without destroying team cohesion.
rounds.coaching_moment: This is a classic 'scope creep' situation. The hardest part is not finding the right answer — it is deciding whose concern to honor when you cannot honor all of them.

choices.label: Negotiate scope reduction with the PM — keep only 3 of the 12 features
choices.feedback: Smart push-back. Alex, Sam, and Jordan all feel heard. Morgan is relieved. The PM is frustrated, but protecting your team was the right call. Strategic leaders say no early and clearly rather than letting scope creep silently poison the project.
choices.coaching_moment: Negotiating scope down is one of the most underrated project management skills. 'No' said early and clearly is a gift — not a failure.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Smart push-back. Alex, Sam, and Jordan all feel heard.

choices.label: Accept all features but pay for overtime to make it work
choices.feedback: Alex is worried about the blown budget. Morgan's morale takes a serious hit — the team is already stressed. Sam and Jordan got what they wanted but the human cost is real. Burning people out to hit dates is a short-term fix with long-term consequences.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Alex is worried about the blown budget. Morgan's morale takes a serious hit — the team is already stressed.

choices.label: Phase the features — launch half now, schedule the rest for v1.1
choices.feedback: Excellent systemic thinking. Phasing lets you deliver value now while protecting quality and team health for the full release. Jordan loves it — you can test properly. Morgan's morale rises because the team sees you protecting them. This is how mature product leaders think.
choices.coaching_moment: Phased delivery is not a failure — it is sophisticated product thinking. The best products ship small and learn fast.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What early signals of scope creep did you notice? How might a leader catch this even earlier?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Bug vs. Deadline Standoff
rounds.story: Three days to launch. Jordan found a critical bug that will take two days to fix properly, or 4 hours to patch imperfectly. Sam says any delay breaks the client contract and risks a €50K penalty. Alex points out the patch costs nothing but a proper fix costs €8K in engineering time. Morgan says the team has been working nights and needs a win — 'just ship it and fix it post-launch.'
rounds.goal: Balance short-term delivery pressure against long-term product integrity.
rounds.coaching_moment: The pressure to ship is real and valid. But 'ship and fix' often means 'ship and never fix' — the next crisis always feels more urgent.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever rushed something important and regretted it later? What would you do differently?

choices.label: Delay launch by 2 days, fix properly, renegotiate with client
choices.feedback: Jordan is relieved and respected. The client conversation is hard, but honesty now prevents a worse conversation later. Sam is frustrated — this is fair. But shipping broken software is almost always more expensive than a short delay.
choices.coaching_moment: Every delayed fix compounds. What costs 2 days now will cost 2 weeks post-launch when you're juggling v1.1 demands.

choices.label: Ship the patch now, schedule proper fix for v1.1
choices.feedback: Jordan is visibly unhappy — quality always loses in this scenario. The patch ships. Everyone celebrates. But Jordan files the bug in the tracker as P0, and it lingers for 4 months. This is how technical debt is born.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Jordan is visibly unhappy — quality always loses in this scenario. The patch ships.

choices.label: Ask the team to vote — transparency and shared ownership
choices.feedback: Risky but powerful. Morgan's morale jumps — the team feels trusted. The decision becomes everyone's, reducing blame if things go wrong. However, team votes can be slow and may not produce the best technical answer. Used well, democratic leadership builds extraordinary trust.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Risky but powerful. Morgan's morale jumps — the team feels trusted.

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Underpaid Engineer
rounds.story: Your best engineer, Priya, just told you she has a competing offer for 40% more salary. She wants you to match it within 48 hours or she leaves — taking 3 months of undocumented system knowledge with her. Alex says the budget has no room. Sam says losing Priya now breaks the timeline. Jordan says Priya built the most complex part of the system and her departure is a quality catastrophe. Morgan says the team is watching how you handle this.
rounds.goal: Navigate retention vs. budget vs. fairness to the whole team.
rounds.coaching_moment: Retention crises are leadership tests. Every person on your team is watching how you treat the person asking for more.

choices.label: Match Priya's offer — go to bat for budget override
choices.feedback: Alex is frustrated but respects the call. The rest of the team sees that good work gets rewarded. Priya stays and the institutional knowledge remains. Going to bat for your team — even against budget pressure — is one of the highest-trust things a leader can do.

choices.label: Offer a non-salary package — extra leave, remote work, title change
choices.feedback: Creative and budget-neutral. Priya's decision depends on what she actually values — if it is money, this fails. If she wants flexibility and recognition, this might work. Non-salary benefits are underused levers in retention. The team sees you trying before accepting defeat.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Creative and budget-neutral. Priya's decision depends on what she actually values — if it is money, this fails.

choices.label: Wish Priya well and begin urgent knowledge transfer
choices.feedback: Alex appreciates the budget discipline, but the cost is severe. Sam and Jordan's trust craters — they see the timeline and quality risks clearly. Morgan's morale tanks as the team wonders if they would be treated the same way. This decision sends a message you may not have intended.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Alex appreciates the budget discipline, but the cost is severe. Sam and Jordan's trust craters — they see the timeline and quality risks clearly.

rounds.reflection_prompt: How do you balance an employee's market value against tight budget constraints — and what's the cost of getting it wrong?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The External Pressure Meeting
rounds.story: Your CEO just scheduled a surprise status update with a key investor. She wants a live demo of features that are 60% complete. Alex says over-promising to investors always backfires. Sam says this is an opportunity to lock in funding for v2. Jordan says demoing incomplete work sets a dangerous precedent for quality expectations. Morgan says the team put in incredible effort and deserves to be recognized publicly.
rounds.goal: Balance investor relations against internal team health and product integrity.
rounds.coaching_moment: How you present reality to leadership shapes the room for temperature change later. Leaders who over-promise gain short-term goodwill and long-term credibility damage.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When have you ever over-committed to impress someone? What happened when reality caught up?

choices.label: Present honestly — show what works, name what does not
choices.feedback: Jordan and Alex are deeply relieved. Morgan feels the team's real work is respected, not dressed up. Investor relations built on honesty are more durable. The investor may be disappointed in the moment, but surprised positively at launch. Credibility is a compound asset.
choices.coaching_moment: Radical transparency with investors separates great leaders from spin artists. It is a harder short game but a better long game.

choices.label: Demo only the completed features — no mention of gaps
choices.feedback: A calculated half-truth. Sam is happy — investor confidence helps funding. Jordan is uneasy, knowing the gaps will surface later. This approach works short-term but creates a difficult conversation when the investor encounters the missing parts post-launch.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A calculated half-truth. Sam is happy — investor confidence helps funding.

choices.label: Lead with team achievements — frame gaps as 'strategic phasing'
choices.feedback: Morgan's morale jumps. The investor sees a confident, proud team. Framing gaps as phasing is strategically defensible if you genuinely plan to deliver them. This is good communications leadership — centering what is true while managing narrative thoughtfully.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Morgan's morale jumps. The investor sees a confident, proud team.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Team Conflict
rounds.story: Alex and Jordan had a blowout argument in Slack last night. Alex accused Jordan of gold-plating features and wasting budget on unnecessary polish. Jordan called Alex short-sighted and said cutting quality was 'building tomorrow's liability.' Both have CCed you. Sam says the conflict is slowing the sprint. Morgan says the rest of the team has taken sides and tension is rising. You need to act today.
rounds.goal: Mediate a values conflict between two respected team members without picking sides.
rounds.coaching_moment: Values conflicts are not about personality — they are about different definitions of success. Your job is not to judge who is right, but to create shared language.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time you were in conflict with someone whose values differed from yours. What helped resolve it?

choices.label: Bring Alex and Jordan together — facilitate a structured conversation
choices.feedback: Both feel heard. Morgan's morale recovers as the team sees the conflict addressed professionally, not ignored or escalated. This is leadership by facilitation — one of the highest-leverage things a team lead can do. The relationship does not heal overnight, but the spiral stops.
choices.coaching_moment: Most interpersonal conflicts at work are not personality clashes — they are structural: two people optimizing for different metrics. Surfacing that removes the personal heat.

choices.label: Meet with each person privately — separate coaching conversations
choices.feedback: Safer but slower. Both feel respected with a private conversation. However, the team sees the conflict unresolved in shared channels and the tension lingers. Private coaching is good first step — it may not be sufficient on its own.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Safer but slower. Both feel respected with a private conversation.

choices.label: Set a communication policy — no conflict in public channels
choices.feedback: Rules without resolution do not fix relationships — they suppress them. Alex and Jordan comply but the conflict goes underground. The team senses the suppression. This is compliance, not resolution. Process can help but it cannot substitute for genuine conversation.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Rules without resolution do not fix relationships — they suppress them. Alex and Jordan comply but the conflict goes underground.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Unexpected Success
rounds.story: The beta launch exceeded expectations — 300% more signups than projected. The board wants to accelerate the full launch by 4 weeks. Alex says the extra revenue justifies more spending. Sam says she has been waiting for this moment — time to prove the team can execute under pressure. Jordan says the product is not ready for that scale of traffic. Morgan says the team is already proud — adding pressure now could cause burnout after such a good sprint.
rounds.goal: Manage sudden success and the internal pressure it creates without losing what made you successful.
rounds.coaching_moment: Success creates its own pressure. The hardest leadership moment is sometimes not the crisis — it is the sudden opportunity that tempts you to overextend.

choices.label: Accelerate — the team earned it and the market is hot
choices.feedback: Sam is thrilled. Alex sees revenue potential. But Jordan's concerns about scale readiness are real — 300% traffic spikes can break systems that were not designed for it. Morgan's morale dips because the team just ran hard and needs recovery time. This is classic startup overreach.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Sam is thrilled. Alex sees revenue potential.

choices.label: Expand selectively — open more users but maintain infrastructure limits
choices.feedback: Everyone gets a partial win. Sam is satisfied. Jordan's technical concerns are respected. Morgan sees the team protected. Alex accepts the measured approach. This is sophisticated scaling — ambitious enough to capture opportunity, disciplined enough not to self-sabotage.
choices.coaching_moment: Controlled growth beats explosive growth followed by collapse. The companies that last are those that scale deliberately.

choices.label: Pause — celebrate the success, invest in infrastructure first
choices.feedback: Jordan and Morgan love this. The team gets to breathe after a huge win. Sam is frustrated — timing matters in markets. Alex sees the cost of delay. This is the conservative play — sometimes right, but it requires strong conviction that the opportunity will still be there in 6 weeks.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Jordan and Morgan love this. The team gets to breathe after a huge win.

rounds.reflection_prompt: When unexpected success arrives, what systems do you immediately put in place to sustain momentum without burning out the team?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Credit Problem
rounds.story: The CEO praised the successful launch in a company all-hands — and named only Sam and Jordan by name. Alex, Morgan, and the rest of the team did not get a mention. Alex says this is fine — results matter, not recognition. Morgan says half the team is demoralized because their contributions were invisible. Sam feels awkward being singled out. Jordan suggests publicly correcting the record. You need to decide how to respond.
rounds.goal: Navigate recognition and credit dynamics to preserve team equity and morale.
rounds.coaching_moment: How credit is distributed is one of the most emotionally charged dynamics in team leadership. People remember recognition failures for years.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Has someone ever taken credit for your work or failed to acknowledge it? How did it feel, and how did it affect your motivation?

choices.label: Send a team email recognizing every contributor by name
choices.feedback: Morgan's morale surges. The whole team feels seen. Sam is relieved to share the spotlight. This is visible leadership — you did not have to say anything, but you chose to. Great leaders create a culture where everyone's contribution is visible, not just the loudest voices.
choices.coaching_moment: The most impactful thing a leader can do for morale costs nothing — say people's names when praising work.

choices.label: Thank each person privately — avoid making it a public issue
choices.feedback: Better than silence. But private thanks does not fix the public omission. Morgan appreciates the gesture but still feels the sting of being invisible to leadership. Private and public recognition serve different psychological needs.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Better than silence. But private thanks does not fix the public omission.

choices.label: Let it go — leadership recognition is not the point
choices.feedback: Alex agrees, but Morgan is quietly devastated. Three team members update their LinkedIn the next day. The invisible contributors feel replaceable. Saying recognition does not matter is something people say when recognition consistently benefits them.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Alex agrees, but Morgan is quietly devastated. Three team members update their LinkedIn the next day.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Post-Launch Retrospective
rounds.story: The launch is complete. The board is happy. Now it is time for the retrospective. Alex wants to focus on what cost overruns to avoid next time. Sam wants to analyze what made the timeline succeed and replicate it. Jordan insists on documenting every quality issue for the next cycle. Morgan wants the team to reflect on what it cost them personally and make sure it does not happen again. You facilitate the session.
rounds.goal: Run a retrospective that captures lessons without assigning blame, and honors both the success and the cost.
rounds.coaching_moment: The best retrospectives end with the team feeling smarter and more connected, not defensive. Blame is the enemy of learning.

choices.label: Use Plus/Delta format — what worked, what to change, no blame
choices.feedback: Everyone contributes safely. The team ends the cycle with documented learning and a sense of being heard. Plus/Delta is deliberately designed to prevent the retrospective from becoming a blame session. Morgan is especially moved that the personal cost was named and heard. This is how teams get better.
choices.coaching_moment: Blameless retrospectives are not about avoiding accountability — they are about isolating process failures from personal failures. The distinction drives real learning.

choices.label: Lead with data — timeline charts, budget variance, quality metrics
choices.feedback: Alex, Sam, and Jordan feel productive. The data is useful. But Morgan and the human side of the sprint go unacknowledged. Data-first retrospectives produce process improvements but often miss the people insights. You leave having learned what happened but not how it felt.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Alex, Sam, and Jordan feel productive. The data is useful.

choices.label: Start with personal stories — what was the hardest moment for each person
choices.feedback: Morgan is deeply grateful. The team bonds over shared difficulty. Some team members who rarely speak up share insights that change how the team thinks about the next cycle. Story-based retrospectives build deeper trust than analytical ones — and often surface the most important lessons.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Morgan is deeply grateful. The team bonds over shared difficulty.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking at the full arc of this project, what is the single decision you would make differently — and why?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

transfer_exercises.game_context: You managed four teammates with competing priorities
transfer_exercises.real_world: In your next team meeting, deliberately ask one person whose perspective you usually skip: 'What is your biggest concern about this?'
transfer_exercises.challenge: Before your next team decision, list each stakeholder's primary concern — without assuming what it is. You may be surprised.

transfer_exercises.game_context: You had to balance short-term pressure with long-term team health
transfer_exercises.real_world: Identify one decision you are currently delaying because it will frustrate someone. Make the decision — then explain your reasoning directly to that person.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Map the stakeholders in one current project. Rate each person's concern level (1-10) and identify who is most at risk of feeling unseen.

cultural_context: Financial literacy is a critical gap in India, where personal finance education is largely absent from school curricula. Team Crisis Manager builds the economic reasoning that prepares Indian students for informed financial decision-making as adults.
coaching_moment: Understanding how others feel and think is the foundation of every great relationship and team.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Team Crisis Manager Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 4 rounds of Team Crisis Manager. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

library.title: Lead engineer resigns mid-incident
library.body: Your tech lead just gave 2 weeks. The team is already burning out from this crisis.

response_choices.label: Ask one honest question: 'what would have made you stay?'

library.title: Largest customer threatens churn
library.body: Your top 3-account-by-revenue is threatening to leave over the same incident. CSM is on the line.

response_choices.label: Have CEO personally call within the hour
Send an IC engineer who knows their stack

library.title: Press is writing about your outage
library.body: A reporter has the broad strokes and is publishing in 4 hours.

response_choices.label: Publish your own honest postmortem first
Route through corporate PR; talking points only

hallmarks: Stabilizes the team before performing for the customer
Asks why-someone-quit honestly instead of negotiating up
Owns the outage publicly before someone else gets to frame it
Distinguishes between fatigue and disengagement — treats them differently
Moves first when ambiguity is highest, even without complete data
Solves the customer-facing crisis while the internal one festers
Reflexively counter-offers when the real signal is 'I'm done'
Hides behind PR when honesty would be cheaper
Sets discount-as-default for retention; loses long-term margin and respect
Confuses being busy with being effective

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
